entities.summary: Charles Louis Auguste Fouquet, duc de Belle-Isle was a French general and statesman who played a crucial role in the Seven Years' War (1756-1763), leading the French forces to several victories in North America, including the capture of Fort Duquesne (present-day Pittsburgh), which gave France control over the Ohio River Valley. Fouquet's military successes were largely due to his collaboration with the British, with whom he had a long-standing alliance, and his strategic use of mercenary troops and Native American allies. His legacy as a military commander and statesman was cemented by his appointment as Governor-General of French Canada in 1761, a position he held until his death in 1761. Fouquet's influence on French politics was also significant, as he was a key figure in the French Enlightenment and a strong advocate for the rights of the common people. He was a prolific writer and published several works on military strategy and politics, including 'Stratégie pour la guerre de 1756' (Strategy for the War of 1756). Fouquet's impact on world history was significant, as he played a key role in shaping the balance of power in North America and Europe during the 18th century. His legacy continues to be studied by historians today, who seek to understand the complexities of his military campaigns and the implications of his policies on the French and British empires.
